Four datasets can share summary statistics and still tell very different stories. Each panel uses the observations published in Anscombe's quartet.

```chart
type: scatter
title: A summary cannot show you the shape
data: { csv: data/anscombe.csv }
encoding: { x: x, y: y, facet: set }
annotations:
  - { kind: text, at: { x: 8, y: 13 }, text: 'y = 3.00 + 0.500x' }
axes:
  x: { label: x }
  y: { label: y }
```

*Source: F. J. Anscombe, “Graphs in Statistical Analysis”, The American Statistician (1973), via the R datasets package.*

```metric
value: "0.816"
label: Correlation between x and y in sets I, II and III; set IV rounds to 0.817
```

- **Set I** is the case the summary describes: points scattered around a straight line.
- **Set II** is a smooth curve. A straight line is the wrong model, however well it scores.
- **Set III** is ten points on a straight line and one point off it. Without the point at x = 13 the fit is y = 4.01 + 0.345x and the correlation is 1.000.
- **Set IV** has ten points at x = 8 and one at x = 19. That one point sets the whole slope; without it there is no slope to fit.

## Almost the same summary

The published observations are rounded, so the fitted values differ slightly. The means and x variance agree at the precision below; the small differences in y variance and correlation remain visible. Each rounded fitted relationship is y = 3.00 + 0.500x. The annotation repeats that shared rounded fit in each panel; it is not an extra set of observations.

| Statistic | Set I | Set II | Set III | Set IV |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mean x | 9.00 | 9.00 | 9.00 | 9.00 |
| Sample variance x | 11.0 | 11.0 | 11.0 | 11.0 |
| Mean y | 7.50 | 7.50 | 7.50 | 7.50 |
| Sample variance y | 4.13 | 4.13 | 4.12 | 4.12 |
| Correlation r | 0.816 | 0.816 | 0.816 | 0.817 |

## The forty-four observations

Sets I to III share their x values; set IV has its own. Read down a column and the difference is hard to see, which is Anscombe's point: the table holds everything the charts show, and still does not show it.

```table
title: Anscombe's quartet as published
data:
  inline:
    - { x: 10, y1: "8.04", y2: "9.14", y3: "7.46", x4: 8, y4: "6.58" }
    - { x: 8, y1: "6.95", y2: "8.14", y3: "6.77", x4: 8, y4: "5.76" }
    - { x: 13, y1: "7.58", y2: "8.74", y3: "12.74", x4: 8, y4: "7.71" }
    - { x: 9, y1: "8.81", y2: "8.77", y3: "7.11", x4: 8, y4: "8.84" }
    - { x: 11, y1: "8.33", y2: "9.26", y3: "7.81", x4: 8, y4: "8.47" }
    - { x: 14, y1: "9.96", y2: "8.10", y3: "8.84", x4: 8, y4: "7.04" }
    - { x: 6, y1: "7.24", y2: "6.13", y3: "6.08", x4: 8, y4: "5.25" }
    - { x: 4, y1: "4.26", y2: "3.10", y3: "5.39", x4: 19, y4: "12.50" }
    - { x: 12, y1: "10.84", y2: "9.13", y3: "8.15", x4: 8, y4: "5.56" }
    - { x: 7, y1: "4.82", y2: "7.26", y3: "6.42", x4: 8, y4: "7.91" }
    - { x: 5, y1: "5.68", y2: "4.74", y3: "5.73", x4: 8, y4: "6.89" }
columns:
  - { key: x, label: "x, I–III", align: right }
  - { key: y1, label: "y, I", align: right }
  - { key: y2, label: "y, II", align: right }
  - { key: y3, label: "y, III", align: right }
  - { key: x4, label: "x, IV", align: right }
  - { key: y4, label: "y, IV", align: right }
```

*Source: Anscombe (1973), in the row order of the paper. `data/anscombe.csv` holds the same 44 pairs in long form.*

## A second distribution

Old Faithful is a geyser in Yellowstone National Park. Each observation pairs the length of one eruption with the wait until the next.

```image
src: media/old-faithful-eruption.jpg
alt: "Old Faithful geyser in full eruption under a dark sky, with visitors watching from the boardwalk"
caption: "Old Faithful in eruption, Yellowstone National Park, October 2019. Photo: NPS / Jim Peaco."
width: 1344
height: 872
```

*Image: [National Park Service, NPGallery](https://npgallery.nps.gov/AssetDetail/9c858b86-9cdb-4bb0-8c17-ea567391faa2), "Old Faithful Geyser, Upper Geyser Basin", NPS/Jim Peaco, 2019; public domain.*

Old Faithful's waiting times and eruptions form two clusters. The **columns** put the paired observations beside the distribution of waits, so you can compare both views.

::: columns

::: column

```chart
type: scatter
title: Longer eruptions accompany longer waits
data: { csv: data/old-faithful.csv }
encoding: { x: waiting_min, y: eruption_min }
axes:
  x: { label: Waiting time, unit: min }
  y: { label: Eruption duration, unit: min }
```

*Source: Old Faithful geyser data, [R datasets package](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/faithful.html); see Azzalini and Bowman (1990) and Härdle (1991).*
:::

::: column

```chart
type: histogram
title: Waiting times have two peaks, and the mean lies between them
subtitle: The 272 waits in minutes; their mean is 70.9
data: { csv: data/old-faithful.csv }
encoding: { x: waiting_min }
axes:
  x: { label: Waiting time, unit: min }
  y: { label: Eruptions }
```

*Source: the same Old Faithful data.*
:::

:::

The mean wait is 70.9 minutes, and few waits are near it: 32 of the 272 fall between 65 and 74 minutes, against 111 between 75 and 84. One average describes neither kind of eruption.

Open the **expand** for the comparison method.

```expand
title: How the two groups were compared
body: |
  Each observation pairs the length of one eruption with the wait until the next. The analysis treats observations as pairs.

  Across all 272 eruptions the correlation between duration and wait is 0.90. The data hold no eruption between 2.9 and 3.067 minutes, so the report splits the observations at three minutes.

  The correlation falls to 0.29 among short eruptions and 0.37 among long ones. Most of the overall relationship comes from the distance between the two clusters.
```

```table
title: Short and long eruptions, split at three minutes
data:
  inline:
    - { group: "Short, under 3 min", n: 97, share: "36%", eruption: "2.04", wait: "54.5" }
    - { group: "Long, 3 min or more", n: 175, share: "64%", eruption: "4.29", wait: "80.0" }
    - { group: All, n: 272, share: "100%", eruption: "3.49", wait: "70.9" }
columns:
  - { key: group, label: Eruptions }
  - { key: n, label: Number, align: right }
  - { key: share, label: Share, align: right }
  - { key: eruption, label: "Mean duration, min", align: right }
  - { key: wait, label: "Mean wait, min", align: right }
```

*Source: the same Old Faithful data. The split at three minutes is this report's; the data hold no eruption between 2.9 and 3.067 minutes.*

## What to take from both

- **Plot before you summarize.** Each of the five datasets here has a mean, a variance and a fitted line. None of those numbers says whether the data are a line, a curve, a line with one stray point or two clusters.
- **One point can carry a statistic.** Set III's slope and set IV's whole fit depend on a single observation.
- **A correlation can come from groups.** Old Faithful's 0.90 is mostly two clusters far apart.

## Data

Both data files and the photograph travel with the report; `media/SOURCES.md` says where the photograph comes from. `data/anscombe.csv` holds the quartet in long form: set, x and y, 44 rows. `data/old-faithful.csv` holds 272 rows: the eruption's duration and the wait until the next eruption, both in minutes.
